prose_changes.old: After two centuries under Arab governors, an Armenian kingdom was restored under the Bagratid dynasty in the 880s, and with it came a burst of church building and writing. The catholicos — the head of the Armenian church — moved his seat to the royal capital of Ani, whose cathedral, finished around 1001 by the architect Trdat, still stands roofless on the plain. Trdat was regarded well enough that he was called to Constantinople to rebuild the dome of Hagia Sophia after an earthquake brought it down. The period's greatest voice, though, was not an architect but a monk. Gregory of Narek wrote a long sequence of prayers, the Book of Lamentations, of such raw self-accusation and longing that Armenians for a thousand years afterwards kept a copy in the house and read it over the sick. The kingdom ended in 1045, when Byzantium annexed Ani; the Seljuk Turks took the city twenty years after that.
prose_changes.new: After two centuries under Arab governors, an Armenian kingdom was restored under the Bagratid dynasty in the 880s. With it came a burst of church building and writing. The catholicos, the head of the Armenian church, moved his seat to the royal capital of Ani. Its cathedral, finished around 1001 by the architect Trdat, still stands roofless on the plain. Trdat may also have been called to Constantinople to rebuild the dome of Hagia Sophia after an earthquake brought it down. The period's greatest voice, though, was not an architect but a monk. Gregory of Narek wrote a long sequence of prayers, the Book of Lamentations. Its self-accusation and longing are so raw that for a thousand years Armenians kept a copy in the house and read it over the sick. The kingdom ended in 1045, when Byzantium annexed Ani. The Seljuk Turks took the city in 1064.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text records Trdat's work on Hagia Sophia; its source, Stephen of Taron, is not vendored, so the claim becomes 'may also have been called'. 'Twenty years after that' becomes 'in 1064', the year Dulaurier gives for Alp Arslan's capture of Ani (RHC lines 4924-4925). The rest of the paragraph is unchanged in substance, split into shorter sentences so it scores.

prose_changes.old: After the Arab conquests reduced the old Georgian kingdoms to a handful of mountain principalities, the rebuilding of Georgian Christian life happened in the highland province of Tao-Klarjeti, where a monk named Grigol founded the monastery of Khandzta around 782 and, over a very long life, seeded a whole district with monasteries. What makes him unusual for a figure of this period is that we can hear about him from inside. A Georgian monk called Giorgi Merchule wrote his life in 951, and it contains the famous sentence defining Georgia itself as the land where the liturgy is celebrated in the Georgian tongue. The movement also went abroad. Georgian monks were in Palestine, on Sinai and near Antioch, and between 980 and 983 they founded Iviron on Mount Athos, which became a translation house moving books between Greek and Georgian in both directions — one of them, a Georgian retelling of a story ultimately of Indian origin, passed into Greek as Barlaam and Josaphat and from there into most of the languages of Europe.
prose_changes.new: The Arab conquests reduced the old Georgian kingdoms to a handful of mountain principalities. Georgian Christian life was then rebuilt in the highland province of Tao-Klarjeti. There a monk named Grigol founded the monastery of Khandzta around 782. Over a very long life he seeded a whole district with monasteries. What makes him unusual for this period is that we can hear about him from inside. A Georgian monk called Giorgi Merchule wrote his life in 951. It contains the famous sentence that defines Georgia itself as the land where the liturgy is celebrated in the Georgian tongue. The movement also went abroad. Georgian monks lived in Palestine, and probably on Sinai and near Antioch too. Between 980 and 983 they founded Iviron on Mount Athos, a house that turned Greek books into Georgian. It may have worked the other way as well. A Christian retelling of a story from India, the life of the Buddha, may have passed from Georgian into Greek there. As Barlaam and Josaphat, it went on into most of the languages of Europe.
prose_changes.reason: Three claims qualified: Sinai and Antioch ('probably'), the Georgian-to-Greek direction of Iviron's translating, and Barlaam and Josaphat as a Georgian retelling ('may have'). Brosset (1849) supports Georgian monks at Jerusalem and Iviron's Greek-to-Georgian work; Robinson (1893) supports the story's Indian origin and its spread, but not a Georgian original. 'The life of the Buddha' is Robinson's identification. The rest is unchanged in substance, split so it scores.

prose_changes.old: After the Arab conquests reduced the Georgian kingdoms to mountain principalities, a monk named Grigol founded the monastery of Khandzta around 782 and seeded the whole district with monasteries — work we can see from inside because his biographer, Giorgi Merchule, wrote in 951 that Georgia was, above all, the land where the liturgy was sung in the Georgian tongue. Georgian monks later carried the movement to Mount Athos, founding Iviron between 980 and 983 as a translation house that moved books between Greek and Georgian, including a story of Indian origin that passed through Georgian and Greek into most of the languages of Europe as Barlaam and Josaphat.

Georgian monks later took the movement to Mount Athos. Between 980 and 983 they founded Iviron there, a house that turned Greek books into Georgian. Its monks may also have carried a story from India out of Georgian into Greek. As Barlaam and Josaphat, it passed into most of the languages of Europe.
